title: STOMP, STAMP and psychotropic medicines
blurb: Apply STOMP, STAMP and NICE NG11 rules so psychotropic medicines are used for the right reason, reviewed on time and stopped when they do not help.
question: Callum, 35, has a learning disability and started olanzapine six months ago for behaviour that challenges. He has gained 9 kg, coughs at meals and has had no bowel movement for five days. Nobody has reviewed the medicine. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: STOMP (stopping over medication of people with a learning disability, autistic people or both) is an NHS England programme launched in 2016 after concerns that psychotropic medicines were being used to manage behaviour rather than treat illness. STAMP (Supporting Treatment and Appropriate Medication in Paediatrics) followed in December 2018 for children, with the RCPCH, the British Academy of Childhood Disability and the Council for Disabled Children. In plain English: the right medicine, for the right reason, at the right dose, reviewed regularly, with non-drug support first.

head: Group
Example use in LD
Watch for
teach.caption: Anti-seizure medicines for epilepsy are not the target; their use for behaviour is.

teach.body: Consider an antipsychotic for behaviour that challenges only if psychological or other interventions alone have not helped within an agreed time, treatment of coexisting physical or mental health problems has not reduced the behaviour, or the risk to the person or others is very severe. Give it with psychological or other interventions, started by a specialist, single drug at the lowest effective dose. Review effectiveness and side effects after 3 to 4 weeks and stop it if there is no indication of a response at 6 weeks.

teach.caption: PHE guidance: antipsychotics can contribute to, or even cause, dysphagia; they also slow the bowel. MHRA warns clozapine can cause fatal intestinal obstruction.

teach.body: NICE NG54 says specialists should start psychotropic medicines in people with more severe learning disabilities, consult the epilepsy team where an antipsychotic could lower the seizure threshold, and use the lowest effective dose. For people who take an antipsychotic but have no psychotic illness, consider reducing it and document the reasons for continuing at least annually. PRN antipsychotics should be used for as short a time as possible and every use recorded and reviewed.

Callum has had olanzapine for six months without any review, far beyond the 3 to 4 week check NG11 requires. He now shows weight gain, coughing at meals (possible dysphagia) and five days without a bowel movement. The nurse treats the bowel and swallowing concerns as urgent physical health issues, starts a bowel chart, requests SLT assessment and asks the prescriber for an urgent medication review. She also asks the team to revisit his positive behaviour support plan, so any reduction is planned and safe.

teach.text: STOMP is not 'stop all medicines'. Stopping a psychotropic suddenly can cause withdrawal effects and relapse. Reductions are planned with the prescriber, the person and family, gradual and monitored. And a person with a diagnosed mental illness may need the medicine: the question is always whether it is the right medicine for the right reason.

teach.caption: A memory aid built from the STOMP aims, not an official acronym.

items: STOMP (2016) and STAMP (Dec 2018, designed for children) tackle overuse of psychotropics.
NG11: antipsychotics for behaviour only with psychological support, after other approaches or where risk is very severe.
Review at 3-4 weeks; stop if no response at 6 weeks.
Side effects (sedation, dysphagia, constipation, weight gain) can be life-threatening.
Reduce gradually with the prescriber; never stop abruptly on your own.

summary: You can now explain STOMP and STAMP and apply NICE NG11 rules on when an antipsychotic may be used for behaviour that challenges and when it must be reviewed or stopped. You can recognise side effects that raise aspiration and constipation risk and escalate them for a medicines review.

A.q: Grace, 9, is autistic and has a learning disability. She has taken a sedative for sleep and behaviour for two years without review. Which national programme specifically covers medicines review for children like Grace?
options: STOMP
LeDeR
STAMP
CETR
A.why: STAMP (Supporting Treatment and Appropriate Medication in Paediatrics), launched in December 2018, extends STOMP principles to children and young people.

whyNot.0: STOMP is the overarching programme; STAMP is the one designed specifically for children and young people.
whyNot.1: LeDeR reviews deaths, not current medicines.
whyNot.3: C(E)TRs review care to avoid admission, not medicines specifically.

A.q: A family carer asks what STOMP aims to do. Which answer is most accurate?
options: Stop overuse of psychotropics and use them for the right reason
Withdraw every psychotropic medicine from people with a learning disability
Replace antipsychotics with anti-seizure medicines for behaviour
Give families the final decision on all psychotropic prescribing
A.why: STOMP aims to stop inappropriate use of psychotropics: the right medicine for the right reason at the right dose, with regular review and non-drug support.

whyNot.1: STOMP is not anti-medication; some people need psychotropics for diagnosed illness.
whyNot.2: Anti-seizure medicines used for behaviour are themselves psychotropics covered by STOMP.
whyNot.3: Families are involved, but prescribing decisions rest with the prescriber in partnership.

A.q: Zoe, 28, started risperidone for severe self-injury alongside a positive behaviour support plan. Under NICE NG11, when should the antipsychotic be stopped if there is no indication of a response?
options: At 3 months
At 4 weeks
At 12 weeks
At 6 weeks
A.why: NG11 1.8.4: review after 3 to 4 weeks and stop if there is no indication of a response at 6 weeks.

whyNot.0: Three months is too long to continue an ineffective antipsychotic.
whyNot.1: 3 to 4 weeks is the first review point, not the stop point.
whyNot.2: Twelve weeks exceeds the 6-week limit in NG11.

B.q: A GP asks the learning disability nurse about starting an antipsychotic for Ryan, 24, whose behaviour that challenges began a month ago. No functional assessment has been done. What is the best advice?
options: Start a low dose now and review its effect in six months
Start a PRN antipsychotic for use during incidents
Try psychological and environmental approaches first
Start an antidepressant instead of an antipsychotic
B.why: NG11 1.8.2: consider an antipsychotic only if psychological or other interventions have not helped within an agreed time, coexisting problems have been treated, or risk is very severe. A functional assessment comes first.

whyNot.0: Starting without trying other interventions, and reviewing at six months, breaks NG11 on both counts.
whyNot.1: PRN use still needs the same justification and is kept as short as possible.
whyNot.3: Swapping drug class without an indication is still medicating behaviour.

B.q: Molly, 33, has a PRN antipsychotic for agitation. Her records show it was given 14 times last month, mostly at 5 pm. What should the nurse do?
options: Review PRN use, look for triggers and request a medicines review
Ask the prescriber to convert the PRN dose to a regular dose
Continue as prescribed because each dose has been clearly recorded
Give the PRN dose at 4 pm each day to prevent the agitation
B.why: NG11 1.8.4: PRN antipsychotics for as short a time as possible, with use recorded and reviewed. A daily pattern suggests a trigger to address through PBS.

whyNot.1: Regular dosing increases exposure without addressing the cause.
whyNot.2: Recording is required, but frequent use must also prompt review.
whyNot.3: Pre-emptive dosing is routine sedation without a review of the cause.

B.q: Daniel, 27, has a learning disability and epilepsy. His psychiatrist plans to start an antipsychotic for a new psychotic illness. What should be done before starting it?
options: Stop his anti-seizure medicine to avoid interactions
Consult the epilepsy team about seizure threshold
Halve his anti-seizure dose for the first month
Start at the highest licensed dose for quick effect
B.why: NG54 1.9.3: take account of effects on other conditions and consult specialists, for example the epilepsy team about antipsychotics lowering the seizure threshold.

whyNot.0: Stopping anti-seizure medicine risks status epilepticus.
whyNot.2: Reducing anti-seizure medicine raises seizure risk further.
whyNot.3: NICE advises the lowest effective dose.

C.q: Callum, 35, has a learning disability and started olanzapine six months ago for behaviour that challenges. He has gained 9 kg, coughs during meals and has had no bowel movement for five days. There has been no review. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Stop the olanzapine today and inform the prescriber
Request an urgent review of the medicine and his symptoms
Offer a low-fat diet and a laxative and recheck next month
Thicken his drinks and monitor his weight each week
C.why: His symptoms suggest antipsychotic side effects: weight gain, possible dysphagia and constipation, which raise aspiration and obstruction risk. He needs an urgent medical and medicines review, SLT referral and a bowel chart.

whyNot.0: Abrupt stopping can cause withdrawal and relapse; changes are planned with the prescriber.
whyNot.2: A month's delay leaves aspiration and bowel risks unmanaged.
whyNot.3: Thickening without SLT assessment is unsafe, and it ignores the medicine as a cause.

C.q: Ahmed, 50, has a learning disability and has taken haloperidol for 15 years. He has never had a psychotic illness and his behaviour has been settled for years. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Continue unchanged because his behaviour is now settled
Stop the haloperidol at once because there is no psychosis
Switch to a newer antipsychotic with fewer side effects
Consider a gradual, monitored reduction with specialists
C.why: NG54 1.9.7: for people taking an antipsychotic without psychosis, consider reducing it and document reasons for continuing. Reduction is gradual and monitored, with PBS in place.

whyNot.0: Long-term use without a psychotic illness needs active review, not default continuation.
whyNot.1: Sudden withdrawal after 15 years risks withdrawal effects and relapse of behaviour.
whyNot.2: Switching keeps him on an antipsychotic without an indication.

C.q: Oliver, 51, has a profound learning disability and takes clozapine for schizophrenia. He has had no stool for four days, has vomited twice and his abdomen is distended. What should the nurse do?
options: Arrange urgent medical assessment the same day
Give an extra laxative dose and review tomorrow
Withhold his clozapine for a day and observe him
Increase fluids and fibre and repeat the bowel chart
C.why: MHRA warns clozapine can cause intestinal obstruction, faecal impaction and paralytic ileus, occasionally fatal; constipation must be recognised early and actively treated. Vomiting and distension need urgent assessment.

whyNot.1: Waiting a day risks a fatal obstruction.
whyNot.2: Withholding clozapine without medical input does not address possible obstruction and risks relapse.
whyNot.3: Dietary measures are too slow for signs of possible obstruction.

reteach.title: A prescription is a promise to review
reteach.question: If a medicine was started to help with behaviour, what must happen next, and when?

blocks.h: Every start has a stop date
blocks.body: An antipsychotic for behaviour is a trial, not a life sentence. It runs alongside a behaviour support plan, is reviewed at 3 to 4 weeks and stopped at 6 weeks if it is not helping. If it is helping, it is still reviewed regularly and reduced when possible.

blocks.text: Side effects can kill quietly: coughing at meals and missed bowel movements in someone on an antipsychotic are red flags, not minor nuisances.

explain.body: STOMP: NHS England, 2016, people with a learning disability and autistic people (now described as covering all ages, with most of its work in adult services). STAMP: December 2018, designed for children and young people, with RCPCH, BACD and the Council for Disabled Children.

test.q: What does the 'P' in STAMP stand for?
options: Psychotropics
Prescribing
Paediatrics
Practice
test.why: STAMP: Supporting Treatment and Appropriate Medication in Paediatrics.

whyNot.0: Psychotropics are the medicines covered, not the P in STAMP.
whyNot.1: Prescribing is not in the title.
whyNot.3: Practice is not in the title.

explain.h: When an antipsychotic may be considered
explain.body: NG11 1.8.2: after psychological or other interventions have not helped within an agreed time, or coexisting problems have been treated without effect, or risk is very severe. Always alongside psychological support.

test.q: Under NICE NG11, an antipsychotic for behaviour that challenges should be given with which of the following?
options: A second antipsychotic at a low dose
A sedative for use at night time
Psychological or other interventions
An anticholinergic to prevent side effects
test.why: NG11 1.8.2: only offer antipsychotic medication in combination with psychological or other interventions.

whyNot.3: Routine anticholinergics add constipation and other risks.

explain.body: Review effectiveness and side effects after 3 to 4 weeks. Stop if there is no indication of a response at 6 weeks. PRN for as short a time as possible, recorded and reviewed.

test.q: When should the first review of a new antipsychotic for behaviour that challenges take place?
options: After 6 months
After 1 week
After 12 weeks of use
After 3 to 4 weeks
test.why: NG11 1.8.4: review effectiveness and side effects after 3 to 4 weeks.

whyNot.0: Six months is far too late.
whyNot.1: One week is too early to judge effect.
whyNot.2: Twelve weeks is past the 6-week stop point.

explain.body: Antipsychotics and other psychotropics can cause sedation, weight gain, swallowing problems and constipation. PHE guidance names antipsychotics as a possible cause of dysphagia; MHRA warns clozapine can cause fatal bowel obstruction.

test.q: A man on an antipsychotic has started coughing during meals. What is the main risk?
options: Aspiration pneumonia from dysphagia
Hypoglycaemia from reduced intake
Raised prolactin caused by the medicine
Dental decay from a dry mouth
test.why: Antipsychotics can cause or worsen dysphagia; coughing at meals suggests aspiration risk, a leading cause of death in people with learning disabilities.

whyNot.1: Coughing at meals points to swallowing, not blood glucose.
whyNot.2: Prolactin rise does not cause coughing at meals.
whyNot.3: Dry mouth is a side effect but not the urgent risk here.
